story: The fourth block ever for FutureBit Apollo Solo, and its first in 19 months, since March 2025. FutureBit Apollo Solo is the solo pool built into FutureBit's Apollo miners, which mine against their owner's own full node: the winner's own machine built this block, and the whole 3.1542 BTC went to a single address used for the first time.
note: Attributed by its coinbase tag, FutureBit-Solo Apollo, which mempool.space files under FutureBit Apollo Solo; FutureBit's Apollo II announcement (Nov 2023) describes the solo pool built into the device. FutureBit itself announced the win as a FutureBit user's, and CryptoBriefing and CriptoNoticias reported it (Oct 2026); no hashrate was published as of 28 Oct 2026.

hardware: ~200 PH/s — about 1,000 Antminer S21s, per Braiins; industrial scale, not a home rig
story: Braiins Solo's fifth block of 2026, 31 days after its fourth — and not a small miner's. Braiins say the winner had about 200 PH/s on the pool, roughly 1,000 Antminer S21s: roughly a 3% chance of a block each day, so a rig that size expects one every month or so.
note: Braiins' account (t.me/Braiins/903, 11 Oct 2026): about 200 PH/s running Braiins OS, a 1-in-5,084 shot per block, and a 197T winning share, 48% over target. The share is checkable, and this block's hash confirms it: 197.3T against the 132.72T required. The hashrate is their figure, not ours — nothing on-chain shows a miner's size. At that size this is an industrial win, which the record otherwise leaves out; it is listed because it came through a public solo pool, with its size stated.

story: Braiins Solo's fourth block. Solo CKPool, Public Pool and Parasite had each gone five weeks without a win when it landed. At 127.45 T it faced the lowest difficulty of any Braiins Solo block so far — the network had eased from 138.96 T in May.

An untagged block whose whole reward went to a single address — an address that has received exactly one coinbase in its life and nothing else, then spent it. That is what one person getting lucky once looks like on-chain, and no public list records it.
note: Inferred, not declared: the coinbase carries no tag at all, so this is read from the payout pattern — one address, one coinbase ever, 3.1380 BTC received and spent. A pool's payout address shows hundreds of transactions; one of the addresses excluded during this audit had 199 and 1,254 BTC.

story: Twelve days after the previous Solo CKPool win on this list, another lone miner took a block: 3.0938 BTC (98%) to one address, with the pool keeping its 2% fee.
Solo CKPool, the oldest and largest solo pool, sent 98% of another block (3.0978 BTC) to a single address and kept its 2% fee. The finder's hashrate was not publicly reported.

hardware: 360 PH/s rented for 9h 18m — not owned hardware
story: Parasite's second win in three days, inside a single difficulty period — this one on rented hashrate. As with every Parasite block, the finder's address got exactly 1 BTC and the other 2.13 BTC went to the pool to be shared among its miners.
note: Braiins say this one was won on hashrate rented through their marketplace rather than owned rigs: 360 PH/s for 9h 18m, nearly 0.07 BTC (~$4.5K) spent, a ~2.2% shot (1 in 46). The winning share was 400T — 3.15× the network difficulty, which matches this block's difficulty exactly. That is their account, not ours: the coinbase carries Parasite's tag and nothing on-chain shows who rented what. Source: Braiins on Telegram, t.me/Braiins/869, 20 Jul 2026.

story: Parasite Pool's finder-keeps model produced another winner — and did it again three days later. The finder's own hashrate was never publicly reported.

A block mined on somebody's own ckpool instance — the coinbase carries 'ckpool' and the tag '/solo-mined/', which is what a self-hosted solo setup writes by default. No pool registry lists it, so every explorer shows it as 'Unknown' and it appears in no public record of solo wins.
note: Identified by auditing the 141 blocks mempool.space could not attribute to any pool over three months. The coinbase tag is the miner's own declaration, not our inference. Their payout address has received two block rewards in total.

hardware: Bitaxe Gamma — 995 GH/s (~1 TH/s) palm-size open-source miner, ~$150
story: A ~$150 Bitaxe Gamma that had been running for about eight hours took the full coinbase on zero-fee, open-source Public Pool — the second block a lone Bitaxe has ever taken on that pool.

A Solo CKPool win whose finder never said how big they were. The tracker that lists it now shows the same payout address at about 68.7 PH/s on 61 workers (8 Nov 2026): a large operation, not a home rig. 98% of the 3.1553 BTC went to that address; CKPool kept 2%.
note: Corrected 8 Nov 2026: an earlier version said ~1.2 PH/s, which the cited tracker does not show.

story: Parasite Pool's third block in five months — the finder-keeps-1-BTC, rest-shared model keeps producing winners.

hardware: Avalon Nano 3S — 6 TH/s, 140 W desktop miner (~$300)
story: A consumer Avalon Nano 3S — a quiet $300 desktop box — solved a block on Braiins Solo against press-reported per-block odds of about 149 million to one. The exact machine class thousands of hobbyists run at home.
Another ckpool solo solve in the same week the Avalon Nano hit — two separate wins three days apart.

hardware: home miner on an Umbrel node — hashrate not publicly reported
story: Public Pool's seventh block, found through a self-hosted Umbrel home node — the miner's own node built the block that paid them.
Braiins Solo's second block, one day after a Public Pool win — solo blocks landed on different pools on consecutive days.

hardware: home miner — hashrate not publicly reported
story: April 2026 put seven solo-pool blocks on the chain, five of them outside Solo CKPool; this self-hosted Public Pool find was one of them.

Ten days after a NerdQAxe++ won on Noderunners, another board of the exact same open design solved a block on Parasite Pool. Two wins in one month for a 4.8 TH/s desktop device that expects one block in thousands of years.
note: Under Parasite Pool's split model the finder keeps 1 BTC and the remainder is shared across the pool's miners.

story: A hobbyist running roughly 70 TH/s — one to two machines' worth — solved a full block through ckpool's European endpoint against reported 1-in-100,000 daily odds.
One 4.8 TH/s desktop unit, on its own, took the whole reward on the Noderunners solo pool. Its community-calculated odds were about 1 in 3,940 per year — and it won anyway.

hardware: NerdOctaxe — 9.6 TH/s (eight Bitaxe-class chips on one board)
story: An eight-chip open-source board solved a block on Public Pool, one day after a 230 TH/s hobbyist won on ckpool — two small-miner blocks in two days on two different pools.
Roughly 1-in-28,000 odds on any given day, and the 312th solo block found through ckpool since 2014 — proof the wins keep coming, year after year.
A sub-10 TH/s miner solved Parasite Pool's headline block. The finder kept 1 BTC under the pool's split model; the rest was shared across every miner on the pool.
The first confirmed block on Braiins Solo — a third major pool operator's solo tier producing a winner within months of launch.

hardware: home miner on an Umbrel node — hashrate not publicly reported
story: An Umbrel-node home miner on Public Pool — found ten days before Parasite Pool's first headline block. Small pools were winning everywhere that February.

hardware: home miner — hashrate not publicly reported
story: A Public Pool solve three days before Christmas 2025 — the third block mempool.space credits to Public Pool, mined, like the two before it, on a self-hosted Public Pool instance on Umbrel.

SoloPool.com's first block, and still the only one mempool.space credits to it. The pool keeps a 2% fee, and the coinbase shows it: 3.0791 BTC went to the finder's address and 0.0628 BTC to the pool's.
A setup the size of three ageing Antminers — the kind that heats a garage, not a warehouse — took 98% of a 3.13 BTC block against daily odds the press put near 1-in-30,000; CKPool kept 2%.

hardware: ~6 TH/s (per CKpool's administrator; one timeline reports a ~5.4 TH/s Bitaxe-class setup)
story: About 6 TH/s, by CKPool's administrator's count — one of the smallest winners on record — won the 308th solo block found through CKPool since 2014 and kept 98% of the 3.146 BTC.
note: Corrected 8 Nov 2026: reports differ on the hardware; the pool operator's figure is shown.

hardware: NerdQAxe++ Rev 6 in a ~130 TH/s home stack
story: The winning hash came from a NerdQAxe++ Rev 6 in a home stack of six NerdQAxe++ units and an Avalon Q, about 130 TH/s in all, mining to the owner's own Public Pool instance on an Umbrel home server.
note: Corrected 8 Nov 2026: the dollar figure and the pool now follow the cited source.

hardware: Avalon Mini 3 — ~37 TH/s silent home miner
story: A living-room Avalon Mini 3 — the heater-quiet kind, not a farm machine — solved a block just two days after the first NerdQAxe++ win. Small-miner September.

The first block ever found by NerdQAxe++ hardware, hashing through OCEAN's DATUM. Because OCEAN is not a pure solo pool, the finder received a proportional payout rather than the whole coinbase — the silicon still did the thing.
note: Included for the hardware milestone; the payout followed OCEAN's reward model, not finders-keepers.

story: Not a desktop box after all: CKPool's administrator put this winner at about 2.3 PH/s — roughly a 1 in 2,800 chance of a block a day, or one in eight years on average. 98% of the 3.17 BTC went to the miner; the pool kept 2%.
note: Corrected 8 Nov 2026: an earlier version showed another block's hardware.

story: A Solo CKPool block 19 days after a Bitaxe took the 297th. An early report credited a Bitaxe Gamma, but that write-up is no longer online and no other source for it has been found.
note: Corrected 8 Nov 2026: the hardware claim had no surviving source. The block itself remains chain-verified.

hardware: home miner — hashrate not publicly reported
story: Public Pool's early win, in the same March 2025 stretch as the Bitaxe cluster and Gamma blocks — the month small miners went on a run across pools.
The third block from FutureBit Apollo Solo, the solo pool built into FutureBit's Apollo miners, which mine against their owner's own full node.

hardware: ~3.3 TH/s in all; the winning hash came from a 480 GH/s Bitaxe (per CKPool's administrator)
story: About 3.3 TH/s in all, and the winning hash came from one 480 GH/s Bitaxe. It was the 297th solo block found through CKPool; 98% of the 3.15 BTC went to the miner's address and the pool kept 2%.
note: Corrected 8 Nov 2026: the hardware and the dollar figure now follow the cited source.

hardware: a Bitaxe, per a mining analyst quoted by the press (hashrate not reported)
story: Its hardware is uncertain. A mining analyst said a Bitaxe found it, but a Bitaxe seller calls the next month's block, 887,212, only the second Bitaxe block ever. The coinbase reads 'ckpool' and 'xmi' and paid the miner 99.5% of 3.158 BTC through a pool no explorer recognises.
note: Corrected 8 Nov 2026: this entry previously carried block 887,212's hardware and story, and called the coinbase untagged. mempool.space lists the pool as Unknown.

hardware: an Apollo-family miner credited to the 256 Foundation — hashrate not publicly reported
story: An Apollo-family block whose coinbase reads 'mined by 256 Foundation' rather than FutureBit's stock tag. mempool.space files it under FutureBit Apollo Solo because the tag starts with 'Apollo'.
note: Corrected 8 Nov 2026: the cited source credits this block to the 256 Foundation and gives no hashrate; an earlier version said ~3 TH/s.

story: The first block from FutureBit Apollo Solo, the solo pool built into FutureBit's Apollo miners — proof that a quiet desktop node-miner can land one.

hardware: ~3 TH/s Bitaxe-class rig, 19 days into solo mining
story: The first famous Bitaxe-era block. Pool logs showed the address had started solo mining only 19 days earlier and reached ~3 TH/s the day before the win — 1-in-1.2-million daily odds, beaten in under three weeks.

hardware: 86 TH/s weekly average — only 8.3 TH/s online at the solve
story: The third solo block in two weeks that January. The miner averaged 86 TH/s over the week, but at the moment the block was solved only 8.3 TH/s was actually online. The lottery does not check how many tickets you meant to buy.

The block that started the modern legend. One home miner, about one machine of hashrate, 1-in-10,000 odds per day — and a 6.35 BTC block, 98% of it to the miner. Two more solo blocks followed within two weeks.
